entries.subject: AArch64/x86-64: Unify the persistent cosimulation wrappers
entries.message:
AArch64/x86-64: Unify the persistent cosimulation wrappers

armsimulate-persistent and x86simulate-persistent were copies of one
script. They differed only in the legacy command they delegate to, the
architecture and state size they announce, and the unit the legacy
command expects the encoding in: armsimulate takes little-endian 32-bit
words, x86simulate takes bytes.

Replace both with tools/simulate-persistent, which takes the target as
its only argument and derives those four values from it. The byte
regrouping generalizes to reversing the bytes of each unit, which is the
identity for the single-byte x86 unit. The executor defaults and the CI
matrix now name the shared script; cosim_spawn already runs the executor
command through a shell, so the argument needs no further handling.

The only behavioral change is the malformed-code diagnostic, which now
reports the protocol architecture name, so x86 reports
malformed-x86_64-code rather than malformed-x86-code.

entries.subject: Add curve25519 projective x-coordinate scalar multiplication
entries.message:
Add curve25519 projective x-coordinate scalar multiplication

The function curve25519_pxscalarmul[_alt] takes the x-coordinate
of a point P on curve25519 and a 4-word (256-bit) scalar n, and
returns a projective representation (X,Z) of the x-coordinate of
n * P = (X/Z,Y). The point P can be (0,0) and the output will
still be correct. There is no specific encoding for the point
at infinity as input, but Z = 0 when that is the output.

This update also tweaks comments for curve25519_ladderstep[_alt]
to make explicit the assumption in the proof that the initial
point has Z = 1, i.e. is effectively the x coordinate of the
affine form of the point.

entries.subject: Relax ML-KEM alignment preconditions (#427)
entries.message:
Relax ML-KEM alignment preconditions (#427)

This removes two alignment assumptions that are stronger than the x86 ML-KEM
implementations require. mlkem_frombytes uses vmovdqu for loads from input
a, so only its vmovdqa output stores require 32-byte alignment.
mlkem_tobytes has the opposite pattern: its input loads use vmovdqa, while
its output stores use vmovdqu.

The redundant assumption is removed consistently from the core, no-IBT, SysV
subroutine, Windows no-IBT, and Windows subroutine theorem layers. There is no
assembly or C API/ABI change; the formal theorem contracts are strengthened.

Add `needs "{arm,x86}/proofs/base.ml"` to proofs

This patch adds `needs "{arm,x86}/proofs/base.ml";;` to the beginning of every proof file,
instead of externally running this from `run-proof.sh`.

This has several benefits:

1. This makes it clear that proofs require loading `"{arm,x86}/proofs/base.ml"`
in advance, which was not explicitly described in README.

2. When using OCaml REPL, this removes waiting of

`loadt "arm/proofs/base.ml";;` must be run first, which will take a few minutes.
This patch removes the necessity of intervention.

entries.subject: Add custom Montgomery inverse for P-256 prime
entries.message:
Add custom Montgomery inverse for P-256 prime

The new function bignum_montinv_p256 is a "Montgomery domain" variant
of the existing modular inverse function bignum_inv_p256, which seems
often to be better suited to the generally Montgomery-centric field
operations supplied by s2n-bignum for P-256. Given an input x it
returns a z such that x * z == 2^512 (mod p_256), or zero in cases
when x is in {0,p_256}. This does indeed correspond to inversion in
the Montgomery domain because if x == 2^256 * X and z == 2^256 * Z
(both mod p_256) then the congruence x * z == 2^512 (mod p_256) means
that X * Z == 1 (mod p_256). The code is in fact almost identical to
bignum_inv_p256, changing only the starting value for the iterations,
and the proof is very similar.

entries.subject: RISC-V: Add directed RV32 arithmetic cosim cases
entries.message:
RISC-V: Add directed RV32 arithmetic cosim cases

The RV32IM cosimulation campaign previously depended entirely on random
sampling. That gives broad coverage over time, but it leaves x0
behavior, operand aliasing, immediate extremes, and signed wraparound
to chance.

Add a fixed arithmetic prelude before the existing random loop. The new
cases cover `ADD`, `ADDI`, `SUB`, `SLLI`, `SRAI`, `LUI`, `MUL`, and
`MULH`, with explicit checks for x0 destinations and sources,
source/destination aliasing, boundary immediates, shift counts 0 and
31, and signed multiply inputs whose high-word behavior is easy to get
wrong.

The random campaign remains in place unchanged after the directed
prelude, including the existing memory cases. The directed cases count
against the same global case and time limits so CI keeps the same
control surface.

Signed-off-by: Hanno Becker <beckphan@amazon.co.uk>

entries.subject: Update sematests CI to run the ARM simulator
entries.message:
Update sematests CI to run the ARM simulator

This patch updates the 'sematests' CI to run the simulator in parallel.
It is set to 30 minutes by default.

To achieve parallelism, a custom bash script is written and invoked from Makefile
instead of writing everything in Makefile.
This is because there is a challenge in relying on `make -j` to run simulators in parallel.
`make -j` assigns one subprocess for one target object, but in this case,
a simulator does not have any target object that it outputs.
To resolve this, we can create N artifical outputs, but then another challenge
is that in Makefile one cannot get the number of processes given to `-j`. :(
(see also: https://stackoverflow.com/q/5303553/1488216)

`make sematest` always runs the simulators using all cores in CPU.

Also, add '!/bin/bash' to the header of armsimulate.

This problem was found while Carl Kwan was running the simulator on his machine

entries.subject: Add custom Montgomery inverse for SM2 prime
entries.message:
Add custom Montgomery inverse for SM2 prime

The new function bignum_montinv_sm2 is a "Montgomery domain" variant
of the existing modular inverse function bignum_inv_sm2, which seems
often to be better suited to the generally Montgomery-centric field
operations supplied by s2n-bignum for SM2. Given an input x it
returns a z such that x * z == 2^512 (mod p_sm2), or zero in cases
when x is in {0,p_sm2}. This does indeed correspond to inversion in
the Montgomery domain because if x == 2^256 * X and z == 2^256 * Z
(both mod p_sm2) then the congruence x * z == 2^512 (mod p_sm2) means
that X * Z == 1 (mod p_sm2). The code is in fact almost identical to
bignum_inv_sm2, changing only the starting value for the iterations,
and the proof is very similar.

entries.subject: x86: Add VMOVMSKPS, VPMOVZXBD, VZEROUPPER instruction models (#387)
entries.message:
x86: Add VMOVMSKPS, VPMOVZXBD, VZEROUPPER instruction models (#387)

* x86: Add VMOVMSKPS, VPMOVZXBD, VZEROUPPER instruction models

Add semantic models for three x86 AVX instructions needed by
mldsa-native's rej_uniform formal verification:

- VMOVMSKPS: Extract sign bits (bit 31) from each 32-bit lane of a
  YMM/XMM register into a GPR. Used to build a comparison mask after
  VPSUBD rejection testing.

- VPMOVZXBD: Zero-extend bytes to dwords (8->32 bit). Used to expand
  table lookup indices from the VPERMD compaction table.

- VZEROUPPER: Clear upper 128 bits of all YMM registers.

Includes decoder entries, instruction type constructors, semantic
definitions, simulator test cases, and execution dispatch.

Signed-off-by: jakemas <jakemas@amazon.com>

* Model VZEROUPPER correctly: zero upper bits of ZMM0-ZMM15

VZEROUPPER zeros bits 128-511 of ZMM0-ZMM15 while preserving the
lower 128 bits (XMM values). Model this by writing each XMM register's
current value back through the zero-extending XMM component path,
which automatically zeros the upper bits of the containing ZMM register.

* Fix VZEROUPPER cosimulation: use YMM writes instead of XMM

The XMM-based model (XMM := read XMM s) chains through two zerotop
wrappers (zerotop_128 then zerotop_256), creating deeply nested
word_zx terms that the sematest cosimulation tactics cannot simplify.

Write to YMM directly with explicit word_subword/word_zx instead,
which only goes through one zerotop layer (zerotop_256 to ZMM).
Semantically identical: preserves lower 128 bits, zeros upper bits.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* x86: Restrict VMOVMSKPS decode to VEX.256 form only

The instruction semantics only handles the 256-bit (VEX.L=1) case.
Reject the 128-bit form in the decoder rather than silently producing
an incorrect operand size from a 128-bit encoding.

entries.subject: AArch64/x86-64: Exit on cosim traps instead of dumping core (#466)
entries.message:
AArch64/x86-64: Exit on cosim traps instead of dumping core (#466)

Cosimulation deliberately runs instructions that trap on hardware,
such as UNDEFINED encodings. The test binary dies from the signal
before printing anything, and `tools/simulate-persistent` reports the
empty output as `TRAP`.

By default, each such signal also produces a core dump. Many Linux
systems hand core dumps to a crash-reporting program (Ubuntu's apport,
or systemd-coredump), which the kernel starts for every crash even when
core files are disabled, and the dying process is not reaped until that
program has read the dump. With many simulators running in parallel
under `make sematest`, this can delay a reply past the 10s deadline in
`cosim_read_line` and fail the run.

Install handlers for SIGILL, SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGFPE, and SIGTRAP in
both `simulator.c` files that call `_exit(128 + sig)`. The output stays
empty, so the case is still reported as `TRAP`, but no core dump is
produced. The handler uses an alternate signal stack, since the
instruction under test may leave the stack pointer unusable. This also
works under qemu-user, which delivers the signal to the guest handler.

A genuine crash of the harness now also shows up as `TRAP` without a
core file.

Factor wordlist_from_memory out of Keccak proofs and generalize

This moves the construct "wordlist_from_memory" that is used in the
Keccak specifications back into the general background theory,
currently in common/bignum.ml. It now has a generalized word type
instead of being restricted to 64 bits, and hence can be used in
other contexts, though the nicest versions of some theorems hold
when the word size is a multiple of 8 or more generally the total
number of bits in the region is a multiple of 8. In support of
the general background, "wordlist_of_num" is also added, a natural
inverse to "num_of_wordlist".

entries.subject: Arm: Add Neon instructions for mldsa-native `polyz_unpack` (#351)
entries.message:
Arm: Add Neon instructions for mldsa-native `polyz_unpack` (#351)

* Arm: Add TBL2 (2-register table lookup)

Follows arm_TBL for the semantics, extending the lookup table from
128-bit (1 register) to 256-bit (2 consecutive registers) using
word_join. The decoder matches len=01 in the TBL encoding and computes
the second register as Rn+1 via word_add.

Needed for mldsa-native polyz_unpack.

Signed-off-by: Matthias J. Kannwischer <matthias@kannwischer.eu>

* Arm: Add USHL_VEC (Unsigned Shift Left, vector variable shift)

Follows arm_ADD_VEC for the decoder structure (3-register same encoding
with size field) and arm_USHR_VEC for the shift semantics. The shift
amount is the low byte of each Rm element interpreted as signed: positive
values shift left, negative values shift right (unsigned).

Needed for mldsa-native polyz_unpack.

Signed-off-by: Matthias J. Kannwischer <matthias@kannwischer.eu>

* Arm: Add MOVI variants (op=0, cmode=0100 LSL #16 and cmode=1101 MSL #16)

Extend the MOVI instruction to support two 32-bit element variants:
- cmode=0100 (LSL #16): produces imm8 << 16 replicated across lanes
- cmode=1101 (MSL #16): produces imm8 << 16 | 0xFFFF replicated across lanes

Needed for mldsa-native polyz_unpack.

Signed-off-by: Matthias J. Kannwischer <matthias@kannwischer.eu>

entries.message:
Memory safety for ML-KEM rejection sampling functions (#366)

* x86: Fix buffer overread in mlkem_rej_uniform_VARIABLE_TIME

Replace the single movdqu (16-byte load) with movq+pinsrd to load
exactly 12 bytes per loop iteration. The previous movdqu would read
4 bytes past the end of the input buffer on the last iteration when
r8 = buflen - 12, since the 16-byte load extends to buf + buflen + 4.

The pshufb shuffle pattern only references bytes 0-11 of the loaded
XMM register, so loading zeros into bytes 12-15 (via movq zeroing the
upper 64 bits) produces identical results.

* Fix x86 rejection sampling proof, add non-Windows memory safety proof

entries.subject: Handle zero inputs in Weierstrass point additions
entries.message:
Handle zero inputs in Weierstrass point additions

This is analogous to the earlier changes for mixed addition. In a
point addition operation P1 + P2, the cases where P1 = 0 or P2 = 0 are
handled specially (though of course using constant-time selection) as
0 + P2 = P2 and P1 + 0 = P1. More precisely, writing P1 = (x1,y1,z1)
and P2 = (x2,y2,z2), the special-case logic is triggered when
precisely *one* of z1 = 0 or z2 = 0 holds; in the case that both
z1 = 0 and z2 = 0 the standard computation is followed and yields the
"right" result (one with its z coordinate also zero).

entries.subject: Generalize field assumptions in curve25519 proofs so far
entries.message:
Generalize field assumptions in curve25519 proofs so far

This changes only the formal specification and its proof, with the
code itself being unchanged. The previous version of the spec, given
the input X, was degenerate unless there was a corresponding Y in the
prime field F(2^255-19) with the affine point (X,Y) on the curve. But
the curve25519 X-coordinate functions like x25519 are explicitly
intended to work even on X inputs where the only suitable Y lives in
an extension field, and the new specification is general over all
fields of characteristic 2^255-19. This includes in particular the
quadratic extension F(2^255-19)[sqrt(2)], which has square roots for
all elements of the prime field and is used in Bernstein's original

  https://cr.yp.to/ecdh/curve25519-20060209.pdf

entries.subject: Fix x86 Curve25519 Mach-O table references (#446)
entries.message:
Fix x86 Curve25519 Mach-O table references (#446)

* Fix x86 Curve25519 Mach-O table references

* Fix x86 Edwards25519 Mach-O table references

Apply S2N_BN_SYMBOL to the remaining x86 base-table references so they
match the underscore-prefixed definitions on Mach-O. The tables are
defined as S2N_BN_SYMBOL(..._constant), which is "_..._constant" on
Mach-O, but were referenced by the bare name. That resolves on ELF,
where both spellings collapse to the same symbol, and leaves the table
undefined when linking on Darwin:

  Undefined symbols for architecture x86_64:
    "edwards25519_scalarmulbase_constant", referenced from:
        _edwards25519_scalarmulbase in edwards25519_scalarmulbase.o

This is the same defect as the preceding commit, covering the four
functions whose tables were moved to .rodata in #413 and #414 rather
than #242: edwards25519_scalarmulbase{,_alt} and
edwards25519_scalarmuldouble{,_alt}. Both are public API, so x86_64
macOS consumers hit it the same way.

The AT&T sources are regenerated with x86_att/attrofy.sed rather than
edited by hand. There is no ELF change: the objects are byte-for-byte
identical for both native and Windows ABI modes, so the HOL Light
proofs, which read the ELF objects via define_assert_relocs_from_elf,
are unaffected and need no regeneration.

* Add Mach-O symbol checking to CI

The preceding two commits fix the same defect twice because no CI job
can see it. S2N_BN_SYMBOL(x) expands to "_x" on Mach-O and to "x"
everywhere else, so a symbol defined through the macro but referenced
bare is only undefined on Darwin. Every x86 job runs on ubuntu-24.04
and builds ELF, where the two spellings are indistinguishable.

Nor is Mach-O covered on the ARM side: s2n-bignum-tutorial-macos-arm
runs "make tutorial", whose TUTORIAL_OBJ list pulls in 2 of the 348 ARM
library sources. The ARM ports are in fact clean today, since they
already guard @PAGE/@PAGEOFF under __APPLE__, so the check is purely a
regression guard there.

Add two complementary checks, as a matrix over both architectures:

  - tools/check-symbol-refs.py flags any symbol defined via
    S2N_BN_SYMBOL that is also referenced by its bare name. It is a
    static text check, so it covers both assembler dialects and needs
    no toolchain. Run against the pre-fix tree it reports all 16
    offending references.

  - The job then assembles each source as Mach-O and requires "nm -u"
    to be empty. Note that "make" alone would not catch this, because
    neither the assembler nor ar resolves symbols; only the undefined
    symbol assertion does.

macos-latest is arm64, so ARM assembles natively and x86
cross-assembles. Nothing is executed, so this needs neither an Intel
runner nor Rosetta. A native Intel runner would additionally allow
linking and running the x86 code, which is stronger, but Intel macOS
runners are on a deprecation path and the x86 Makefile path has not
been exercised under Apple's assembler.

Only the Intel dialect is assembled for x86: x86_att is already proven
object-identical by the s2n-bignum-tests job, and it uses GNU as macro
semantics that clang's integrated assembler rejects. The tutorial and
proofs trees are excluded as HOL Light scaffolding rather than library
code.

entries.subject: Add custom Montgomery inverse for P-384 prime
entries.message:
Add custom Montgomery inverse for P-384 prime

The new function bignum_montinv_p384 is a "Montgomery domain" variant
of the existing modular inverse function bignum_inv_p384, which seems
often to be better suited to the generally Montgomery-centric field
operations supplied by s2n-bignum for P-384. Given an input x it
returns a z such that x * z == 2^768 (mod p_384), or zero in cases
when x is in {0,p_384}. This does indeed correspond to inversion in
the Montgomery domain because if x == 2^384 * X and z == 2^384 * Z
(both mod p_384) then the congruence x * z == 2^768 (mod p_384) means
that X * Z == 1 (mod p_384). The code is in fact almost identical to
bignum_inv_p384, changing only the starting value for the iterations,
and the proof is very similar.

Add single-register case of TBL instruction to ARM model (#219)

* Add single-register case of TBL instruction to ARM model

This instruction uses the bytes in one argument as indices into the
bytes in the other one. Any indexing bytes >= 16 result in a zero
result for that lookup, by definition, and this is implicit in the
definition of the semantics using "word_subword". Note that our
cosimulation testing in "simulator.ml" with random numbers will have
a strong bias towards this trivial case for each lookup. However,
there's around a 50% chance that at least one of the 8 or 16 lookups

seems that it still gives adequate coverage.

"arm_TBL Q29 [Q14] Q17 128", which makes the abstract syntax look
more like the ARM assembler language while also allowing for a
natural extension in the future to multi-register cases.

Add byte-level interfaces for X25519 functions

These provide alternative interfaces at the C level, with "_byte" in
their names to distinguish them, treating the arguments as arrays
of bytes (uint8_t) rather than of 64-bit words (uint64_t). This
better reflects how the X25519 function is generally specified and
used.

  void curve25519_x25519_byte(uint8_t res[static 32],uint8_t scalar[static 32],uint8_t point[static 32]);
  void curve25519_x25519_byte_alt(uint8_t res[static 32],uint8_t scalar[static 32],uint8_t point[static 32]);
  void curve25519_x25519base_byte(uint8_t res[static 32],uint8_t scalar[static 32]);
  void curve25519_x25519base_byte_alt(uint8_t res[static 32],uint8_t scalar[static 32]);

The underlying code is exactly the same in the x86 case, since
the platform is guaranteed to be little-endian, and the proofs
just rephrase the same results in terms of byte arrays.

The ARM functions are actually different code, using byte-level
loads and stores (ldrb, strb) at the beginning and end, and so
their proofs are also slightly different.

entries.subject: Arm: Model narrowing shifts: SQSHRUN, SQRSHRUN, and RSHRN (#432)
entries.message:
Arm: Model narrowing shifts: SQSHRUN, SQRSHRUN, and RSHRN (#432)

* Arm: Add SQSHRUN and SQSHRUN2

Add signed-to-unsigned saturating narrowing shifts. Each source lane is
shifted arithmetically, clamped to the unsigned range at half its width,
and written to the low or high destination half.

Decode SQSHRUN within the modified-immediate owner so immh = 0 remains
available to valid immediate encodings. Register the expanded rules and
add simulator coverage for legal and reserved sizes.

* Arm: Add SQRSHRUN and SQRSHRUN2

Add the rounded signed-to-unsigned saturating narrowing shifts. Apply
the rounding offset before the arithmetic right shift, then clamp each
lane to the unsigned range at half its width.

Keep the decoder disjoint from modified-immediate encodings, reject
reserved source sizes, register the expanded rules, and add simulator
coverage for both forms.

* Arm: Add RSHRN and RSHRN2

Add non-saturating rounded narrowing shifts. Treat each source lane as
unsigned, apply the rounding right shift, and truncate the result to
half its original width.

Decode valid immediate shifts, reject reserved source sizes, register
the expanded rules, and add simulator coverage for the base and high
destination-half forms.

entries.subject: Maintain a list of specification theorems and check against it
entries.message:
Maintain a list of specification theorems and check against it

Currently `make proofs` checks that all specifications are proven by
comparing the number of appearances of `let [A-Z_0-9]*_SUBROUTINE_CORRECT`
in the `proofs/*.ml` files with respect to `SUBROUTINE_CORRECT : thm` in
`*.correct` output files.

It seems this can be fixed to be more robust, by addressing these concerns:

- Simply comparing the numbers is not as strong as comparing the exact list
  of specifications (between those to be proven and are actually proven)
- If a patch is large, an author might mistakenly remove/rename a
  specification and a reviewer might miss it as well. However, the current
  checker does not raise an alarm in this case.

This patch adds two text files that contain explicit lists of specifications
that must be proven for each architecture.
The list for {Arm,x86} is located at `{arm,x86}/proofs/specifications.txt`.
These can be generated by `tools/collect-specs.sh {arm,x86} > {arm,x86}/proofs/specifications.txt`.

An author has to update these files if new specifications are added to s2n-bignum.
On the other hand, on the reviewers' side, looking into these files is enough to
confirm that the reviewing patch adds/removes specifications. :)

entries.subject: Modify specification style for Weierstrass curve point operations
entries.message:
Modify specification style for Weierstrass curve point operations

The previous specifications proved that, assuming none of the usual
degenerate cases, the results correspond to "canonical" Jacobian
operations, with specific encoding of the point at infinity as
(1,1,0). However, this canonical form seems to have little or no
implementation value and any interesting conclusions are excluded by
the exceptions in the precondition.

The new specifications are stated in terms of the mapping back to
affine form, for which any triple of the form (x,y,0) is treated as
the point at infinity. This already removes all special cases from
doubling and removes one of the four special cases from addition,
namely x + -x' = 0 where x' and x are projectively equivalent. The
new specifications are also perhaps a bit more compact and easily
understood.

entries.subject: Add read-only section support for ELF AArch64 (#207)
entries.message:
Add read-only section support for ELF AArch64 (#207)

* Add read-only section support for ELF AArch64

This patch adds support for reading the read-only section of ELF (AArch64)
and using it.

This is achieved by extending the ELF loader to
(1) find the .rodata section and read it
(2) read the symbol table and find the objects that are defined in `.rodata`
(3) read the relocation info to record which instructions must be updated when loading it.

For ELF AArch64, GCC is typically using `adrp` + `add` combination (which is also
equivalent to the `adrl` pseudoinstruction) to add the PC-relative offset
and correctly find the symbol address.

When relocation is involved, the machine-code isn't just a list of bytes, but
in fact a function that takes the virtual addresses of the symbols and returns the
correct, 'patched' machine code (which is a byte list).
`define_assert_relocs_from_elf` returns that, as well as a list of new definitions
describing the contents of constant data.

This patch also includes `arm/tutorial/symtab_rodata.ml`, which is an example that loads
constant data.

I found that the following references were helpful:
- https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aaelf64/aaelf64.rst#5733relocation-operations
  for overall meanings of AArch64-specific relocations
- https://refspecs.linuxbase.org/elf/gabi4+/ for the structure of an ELF file
- https://github.com/lattera/glibc/blob/master/elf/elf.h#L2731 for kinds of relocations

* maychange events, etc

* Fix a bug in dstreg masking, add save_literal_relocs_from_elf

* fix incorrect sanity check that was added, remove too inclusive try-with

The in-range sanity check that was introduced to `get_int_le` was incorrectly failing in some cases.
This was caught by a too inclusive try-with expression in `load_elf`, causing it to
return an empty list of constant symbols when any expression in it failed.
Removed the try-with expression, and instead adopted the 'catch' function and specifically used it.

* add function g(i) that calls f(i+z) and prove its spec

* fix a failure in sematest

cosimulator was giving `REFL ibytecode` to `ARM_MK_EXEC_RULE`, and applying `REWRITE_RULE` to ths REFL term was too eagerly folding it into true. Use `PURE_REWRITE_RULE`

entries.subject: AVX2 instructions needed for ML-KEM code (#291)
entries.message:
AVX2 instructions needed for ML-KEM code (#291)

* Add VMOVDQU to x86 model

This also fixes an error in read_VEX, which was not correctly
analyzing the implicit prefix parts in the case of a 2-byte
VEX prefix, only doing so in the 3-byte case.

* Add VPOR to the x86 model

* Add VPSLLW to x86 model

* Add VPSLLD and VPSRLD (usual immediate third operand) to x86 model

* Add VPBLENDW to the x86 model

This also enforces the ".W0" (VEX.W = 0) restriction on the existing
decoding of VPBLENDD. For the new VPBLENDW by contrast, the field is
ignored so there are acceptable encodings with an extra bit set.

* Add VPERMD to x86 model

* Add VPSHUFB to x86 model

* Tighten up some W0 and W1 restrictions on AVX2 instructions

Many of these are to be decoded as "WIG", i.e. the W field ignored,
but a few require a specific setting 0 or 1 for the W field according
to the manual. This makes sure we don't accept other settings, which
are probably illegal or distinct instructions.

* Refine implicit prefix requirements on AVX2 instructions

This tightens up the decoding to require the actual implicit
prefixes as specified in the manual by pattern-matching over
the "pfxs" field extracted by read_VEXP. The correspondence
with the notation in the manual is:

    (T, Rep0, SG0) corresponds to VEX.nnn.66
    (F, RepZ, SG0) corresponds to VEX.nnn.f3
    (F, RepNZ, SG0) corresponds to VEX.nnn.f2

Having these additional matching clauses at the inner level
is a bit verbose, particularly since the "0x66" cases are in the
majority, but doing the decision tree in another way would
only be slightly shorter and probably harder to read.

* Fix sizes of memory operations in VPBROADCAST semantics

These have different sizes for destination and source and so
they need a bit more delicacy in decoding.

* Enforce VEX.LZ restriction in MULX decoding

As pointed out by Yan Peng, this ought to be checked, otherwise
we are quietly accepting a fake instruction that should cause
an undefined instruction exception on hardware.

* Add newly introduced AVX2 instructions to x86 allowed_asm list

This patch rewrites the proofs of correctness of bignum_mul_8_16_neon and bignum_sqr_8_16_neon using program equivalence proof.
Their `*_SUBROUTINE_CORRECT` theorems (which are the most important theorems) remain unchanged. The only differences are that
their proofs rely on the program equivalence between their scalar versions and Neon versions.

To define program equivalence and prove related lemmas, this patch adds a bunch of definitions and lemmas in the following new files:
- `common/relational2.ml`: This file defines relational Hoare logic for machine code as a new predicate `ensures2`.
This internally uses a new predicate called `eventually_n`.
This file also defines a unary Hoare logic predicate `ensures_n` which uses `eventually_n` in contrast to `eventually` which is used by `ensures`.
Finally, this file proves several properties on `ensures2`, `ensures_n` and `ensures`.
- `arm/proofs/equiv.ml`: This file includes simulation tactics for a pair of programs. Also, this includes tactics and lemmas that enable conversion between Arm `ensures_n` and `ensures` because this is important to 'induce' the final specification from equivalence and original specification
- `tools/diff.py`: This is a Python script that prints the diff lines between two assembly files as an OCaml list of tuples. This is in turn used by `EQUIV_STEP_TAC`.

This patch only targets use cases in Arm, but `common/relational2.ml` is designed to be reusable for x86 assembly programs as well.

entries.subject: Add modular square root for curve25519 field
entries.message:
Add modular square root for curve25519 field

The calls bignum_sqrt_p25519(z,x) and bignum_sqrt_p25519_alt(z,x)
compute in z the square root modulo 2^255-19 of the input x, returning
(as a signed integer, type int64_t) the corresponding Legendre/Jacobi
symbol:

    0: x is divisible by 2^255-19 and z is the square root (zero)
   +1: x is coprime to 2^255-19 and z is a square root
   -1: x is coprime to 2^255-19 but has no modular square root

Thus, the result written to the z buffer is a modular square root
mod 2^255-19 whenever one exists, i.e. whenever the Legendre symbol
is >= 0. The even (LSB=0) square root is always chosen.

entries.message:
Add 256-bit and 384-bit big-endian conversions

The functions are called "bignum_bigendian_4" (4 words = 256 bits) and
"bignum_bigendian_6" (6 words = 384 bits), with additional aliases
using names "...frombytes..." and "...tobytes...", treating either
input or output as a byte array (exactly the same code, but with a
different type in the C prototype). Each such alias has its own
variant correctness theorem stated slightly differently.

Although they are not specific to the P-256 and P-384 primes (only
their native sizes) they are located in the respective "p256" and
"p384" subdirectories, since the main anticipated uses are in
connection with those primes.

For a little-endian platform, these always amount to byte reversal.
The ARM code has not been tested in a big-endian instantiation, and
since the current ARM model assumes little-endianness a priori,
neither has it been verified in a big-endian setting, but it is
supposed to work there. This is not relevant for x86, which is always
little-endian.

Fix several BSD portability issues

A few aspects were previously only reliable on Linux or Mac OS:

 * The choice of the two different relocation syntaxes for ARM
   is really just an ELF versus Mach-O difference, so the extra
   defined(__linux__) guard is now removed.

 * We don't want to explicitly include alloca.h on BSD, and in
   fact we don't need to do it on Mac OS either, so it's now
   guarded by __linux__.

 * The method of querying for the existence of SHA3 hardware on
   ARM is slightly different on BSD.

So far this has only been tested with FreeBSD 14 on ARM, but it
is hoped it will work on OpenBSD and other versions too.

entries.subject: x86 uniform rejection sampling for ML-KEM, MOVSB and related additions (#320)
entries.message:
x86 uniform rejection sampling for ML-KEM, MOVSB and related additions (#320)

This adds the x86 rejection sampling code from mlkem-native with a
couple of minor changes, and its correctness proof. The correctness
proof is in effect a simplified version of the ARM proof, with the
same kind of underlying logic but much simpler loop structure. The two
changes to the code are:

- Directly test for null input (buflen = 0), and skip the body and
  return 0 in that case.

- Use xmm3 in place of xmm6, so we don't need to save/restore it
  for Windows

The more complicated side of this update is the setup of
infrastructure to support a single instruction REP MOVSB, which is
used as the last step of the code to copy from the temporary buffer on
the stack to the output. This is rather different from all the x86
instructions formalized so far in that it manipulates
arbitrarily-sized buffers of memory, not just individual chunks 8, 64,
256 bits or whatever. Moreover the semantics is explicitly sequential,
and handling the case of overlapping input and output buffers needs to
take account of this. An auxiliary function x86_movsb is defined
recursively, and for simulation this is factored into an equivalent
using x86_stringcopy with bounded input and output buffers.

A second level of additional work is needed because repetition inside
REP MOVSB is controlled by the DF flag, not previously part of the x86
formalization (this determines whether iteration is downward or
upward). We add this to the model and the simulator, as well as the
two instructions for explicitly setting and clearing it (CLD, STD).
Finally, all the MOVSB and REP MOVSB semantics is checked in the
simulator for sizes up to 7 bytes, which should be enough to exercise
the various corner cases.
